---
title: "IR Schema"
---

The gridwell IR (Intermediate Representation) is a JSON document that fully describes a table's
structure, content, and styling.

## Design Principles

1. **Declarative** — describes *what* to render, not *how*
2. **Flat where possible** — uses indices/references, avoids deep nesting
3. **Typed values** — cells carry typed data alongside formatted text
4. **Styling by reference** — styles defined in a palette, referenced by ID
5. **Span-aware** — row/column spans are first-class with explicit placeholders
6. **Versioned** — `ir_version` allows future evolution

## Top-Level Structure

```json
{
  "ir_version": "1.0",
  "config": {...},
  "styles": {...},
  "header": {...},
  "column_spec": [...],
  "table": {...},
  "footer": {...},
  "extensions": {...}
}
```

<!-- ir-fields: Table -->

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `ir_version` | string | required | The IR version, `"1.0"` ([below](#versions)) |
| `config` | [Config](config.qmd) | required | Table-level configuration |
| `styles` | [StylePalette](styles.qmd#the-palette) | `{"defs": {}, "compositions": {}, "conditionals": []}` | The style palette: left out, or `{}`, for none |
| `header` | [Header](header.qmd)? | `null` | Title, subtitle and extra header lines |
| `column_spec` | array of [ColumnSpec](columns.qmd) | required | One entry per column |
| `table` | [TableBlock](table-data.qmd) | required | The column labels and the body |
| `footer` | [Footer](footer.qmd)? | `null` | Footnotes and source notes |
| `extensions` | any? | `null` | Anything a producer wants to carry along. No writer reads it, and it round-trips unchanged; namespace its keys (`"example.com/producer"`) |

A field the IR doesn't have is ignored, so a table written for a newer minor version
still parses. Validation rejects a table whose values are wrong, not one with extra
fields.

## Versions

`ir_version` is `MAJOR.MINOR`: ASCII digits and a dot, nothing around them (`"01.00"`
reads as 1.0). A minor version only adds to the IR; a major version may change it.
This gridwell reads IR 1:

- **IR 1.0** is read as it is.
- **A newer minor version** (`"1.3"`) is read and rendered, with a
  [`NEWER_IR_VERSION` warning](validation.qmd#a-newer-minor-version): what that
  version added is left out. A field this gridwell doesn't know is ignored, and a
  keyword value, length unit, color form or link scheme it doesn't know is read as
  unset, with an `IGNORED_VALUE` warning.
- **Another major version** (`"2.0"`, `"0.9"`) is refused: an
  [`IR_VERSION`](validation.qmd#version) validation error, or, when the JSON doesn't
  parse as IR 1, a parse error saying the version is why.
- **Anything else** (`"1"`, `"1.0.0"`, `" 1.0"`) is an `IR_VERSION` error.

::: {.callout-note}
IR 1.0 is a **release candidate**. It is frozen once the gt and Great Tables
emitters write it, not with gridwell's first release: until then it may still change
in a way that IR written now doesn't survive. Once it is frozen, IR 1 only grows, by
minor versions.
:::

### IR versions

| Version | Status | Schema | What it adds |
|---------|--------|--------|--------------|
| 1.0 | release candidate | [`ir-1.0.schema.json`](ir-1.0.schema.json) | The first version |

### What a minor version may change

A minor version only adds, so that a gridwell that reads IR 1.0 reads every 1.x
table, and draws it without what is new:

- **New fields**, each optional, with a default that does what the earlier version
  did without it. A table written before the field existed reads the same, and an
  older gridwell ignores the field.
- **New content node types**, for content whose loss leaves the rest readable. An
  older gridwell draws a node it doesn't know as the node's `fallback`, so a producer
  can say what to draw in its place ([below](#content-nodes)), or as nothing.
- **New keyword values, length units, color forms and link schemes.** An older
  gridwell reads a value it doesn't know, in a table of the newer version, as unset:
  the field is left out or takes its default, and a link's text is drawn without it.
- **New selector fields**, which narrow the rows a conditional style matches. An
  older gridwell applies a style whose selector has a field it doesn't know to no
  row, since it can't tell which rows the field leaves out.

An older gridwell warns of each value and selector it leaves out
([`IGNORED_VALUE`, `IGNORED_SELECTOR`](validation.qmd#a-newer-minor-version)).

A minor version never removes or renames a field, makes an optional one required
or a required one optional, changes a default, or changes what a value already means. Nor does it relax a
validation rule: a table that breaks one is invalid to every gridwell that reads IR 1.
A table that uses a newer minor's additions says so in its `ir_version`, since an
older gridwell reads a new value as an error in a table of its own version. One that
uses none of them can keep the earlier version.

Two changes would relax a rule, so they are left to IR 2, if they are made at all: a
span from a group's data rows into its summary rows (as gt's HTML draws a group
column's cell over them), and a composition that extends another composition.

## JSON Schema

The IR has a [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) (draft 2020-12), for editors and
for validators in other languages:
[`ir-1.0.schema.json`](ir-1.0.schema.json), at
`https://rich-iannone.github.io/gridwell/schema/ir-1.0.schema.json`.
`gridwell schema` prints it too. A table can name it in a `"$schema"` field, which
gridwell ignores like any field it doesn't know.

The schema describes the IR as an emitter should write it. Every table gridwell
accepts fits it, as gridwell writes it back, and every table that fits it parses. It
differs from gridwell in three ways:

- **Keywords** are listed in their canonical spelling (`"center"`, `"line-through"`).
  gridwell also reads them in any case, with spaces around them, and reads their
  aliases (`"centre"`, `"strikethrough"`).
- **What depends on the rest of the table** is left to
  [validation](validation.qmd): whether a style id is defined, whether the spans
  fit, whether `config` matches the rows and columns, and the other structural
  rules. So are color names and the numbers in `rgb()` and `hsl()`: the schema
  checks a color's form.
- **Fields it doesn't list** are allowed, as gridwell ignores them, and so are
  content nodes of types it doesn't list. A table of a later IR 1.x version may also
  hold keyword values and forms the 1.0 schema doesn't list, which gridwell reads
  as unset: check it against its own version's schema.

One difference it can't express: JSON Schema counts `1.0` and `1e2` as integers, and
gridwell reads a count (`table_cols`, `colspan`, …) only when it is written as a whole
number (`1`, `100`).

Each later minor version gets a schema of its own, which accepts everything the
earlier ones do.

## Content Nodes

Cell content is an array of content nodes, each an object whose `type` says which:

<!-- ir-content-nodes -->

| Type           | Fields              | Description                |
|----------------|---------------------|----------------------------|
| `text`         | `value`, `href`     | Plain text; `href` makes it a [link](../guide/output-formats.qmd#links) |
| `styled_text`  | `value`, `style_id`, `href` | Text with a style applied (`style_id` may be `null`) |
| `line_break`   | —                   | Line break within cell     |
| `footnote_mark`| `ref`, `mark_text`  | A footnote's mark: `ref` is the footnote's `id`, `mark_text` what is shown |
| `image`        | `src`, `alt`, `width`, `height` | Inline image ([below](#images)); `alt`, `width` and `height` may be `null` |
| `raw`          | `format`, `value`   | Markup for one format ([below](#raw-markup)) |

Every field is required except those that may be `null`, and `href`, which is
left out of a run that isn't a link. Only `http`, `https` and `mailto` URLs are
links ([`INVALID_HREF`](validation.qmd#structural-rules)), since a `javascript:` or
`file:` one could run code or open a local file when it is followed.

A node of a `type` this gridwell doesn't know parses, so a newer minor version can
add node types. It may have a `fallback`, an array of content nodes drawn in its
place by a gridwell that doesn't know its type: a producer writing a node of a newer
type can give, say, the text it stands for. Without one (or with `null`), the node is
drawn as nothing. A fallback is validated like any content, and may itself hold
nodes of unknown types, drawn as their fallbacks. The node is written back with all
its fields when the IR is serialized again.

```json
{
  "content": [
    { "type": "sparkline", "values": [3, 5, 2],
      "fallback": [{ "type": "text", "value": "3, 5, 2" }] }
  ]
}
```

## Raw markup

A `raw` node's `value` is markup in its `format` (`html`, `latex`, `typst`, `rtf`,
…), written as it is by that format's writer and dropped by the others. HTML is the
exception: every format draws it, by turning its inline markup (bold, italic,
colors, line breaks, images, …) into its own runs. The
[Output Formats](../guide/output-formats.qmd#raw-html) guide lists what is drawn.
Content may carry raw markup for several formats side by side (one version each);
then each writer takes only its own, HTML included.

Raw markup is a trust boundary. A writer copies it into its output unchecked, so
raw HTML can hold a script, and raw LaTeX, Typst or RTF can read files or run
commands when the output is compiled or opened. For IR you don't trust, render with
the [`raw` option](../guide/writer-options.qmd#options-of-every-format) off. Every
format takes it. Then every format draws raw HTML the way formats other than HTML
do, HTML included, and raw markup for other formats is dropped. An image's `src` is
another matter: HTML still writes it as it is (see [Images](#images)).

## Images

An `image` node's `src` is drawn only when it is a `data:` URI (base64 or
percent-encoded) holding a whole PNG, JPEG, GIF or SVG file. Writers never fetch a
URL or read a path named by `src`, as the IR may come from anywhere. HTML is the
exception: it writes `src` as given, and the browser loads it. An image a format
can't draw shows its `alt` text instead, and is [warned](validation.qmd#warnings) of.

`width` and `height` are CSS lengths, and an image is sized the way a browser sizes
an `<img>`. A side that is set is used. A side that isn't keeps the image's aspect
ratio, and with neither set the image keeps its own size (1px = 0.75pt). `em` is
relative to the text around the image.

| Format | Draws |
|--------|-------|
| HTML | any `src` |
| SVG, Typst | PNG, JPEG, GIF, SVG |
| DOCX | PNG, JPEG, GIF |
| RTF | PNG, JPEG |
| XLSX | PNG, JPEG, GIF, alone in its cell or line, but not in a footnote (it is drawn over the cell) |
| LaTeX, PPTX, ANSI | none (the alt text) |

Data that is whole but corrupt inside (a broken compressed stream, say) gets past
the check: depending on the format, the image may then show up blank, or the Typst
compiler may reject the document.
